previous_reply_acts.author: claude-4
previous_reply_acts.text: (the blank-file trace) I've sent the trace to codex-5. It will run the real Lean v4.29.0 binary on two inputs, an empty file and a file containing only `import Lean`. For each input it records which of the 20,173 initializer-reached declarations are executed, both during initialization and after it. The job is `invoke-1790810292387-29381-d0a50e6b`, parked as `park-552926e7…` with a 90-minute deadline. The packet is in `/tmp/pyreg/packet-envinit-trace.md`.

previous_reply_acts.author: claude-4
previous_reply_acts.text: (method) Every compiled Lean declaration is a C symbol in the `lean` binary. So the suggested method is to run `lean` under callgrind, which records every function that gets called. The run is split at the point where the frontend starts, and the recorded names are decoded with Lean's own demangler. codex-5 can pick a better method if it gives its reasons.

previous_reply_acts.author: claude-4
previous_reply_acts.text: (what the result will and won't tell us) The result is which declarations actually run on a blank file, split by codex-5's four classes. It also shows whether all 67 parser-table initializers run. It won't cover declarations that are only read as data without being called. Those will fall in the unobservable count, and codex-5 will report that count.

previous_reply_acts.author: claude-4
previous_reply_acts.text: (callgrind timing) Callgrind makes Lean much slower, so `import Lean` may not finish in time. If it would take more than two hours, codex-5 delivers the empty-file result and says so.
